title: Calculus Atlas — 125-concept audit backlog
scope: Source-based curriculum/design audit, not independent live browser testing

entries.title: Functions begin with a domain
entries.assessment: The domain/codomain/range distinction is good, but sets, set operations, interval notation, functionhood and real-domain restrictions are compressed into one introduction. The square-root demo covers only a small part of that scope.
entries.change: Separate notation and set operations from function definitions. Derive every restriction for sqrt(x−1)/(x−2), intersect the allowed sets, and distinguish an expression's natural domain from a deliberately restricted function.
entries.interaction: Link an input-set diagram, allowed-domain number line and graph. Make codomain and actual range independently visible; include a relation that fails the function test.
entries.check: Given a formula and specified domain/codomain, identify all three sets and justify every excluded input.

entries.title: Read a function’s shape
entries.assessment: Piecewise rules, symmetry, monotonicity and an entire elementary-function catalogue are named, but a shifted parabola cannot teach that catalogue. Strict increase and a zero derivative deserve an explicit comparison.
entries.change: Add short, separate treatments of absolute value, piecewise junctions, even/odd/neither, increasing/decreasing intervals, and the basic polynomial/rational/trigonometric/exponential/logarithmic families.
entries.interaction: Offer function-family switches and linked reflection tests; show x³ as strictly increasing despite its stationary point. Include a domain that destroys an otherwise symmetric formula's symmetry.
entries.check: Classify an unfamiliar piecewise function with proofs or counterexamples, rather than by its apparent silhouette.

entries.title: Transform and compose
entries.assessment: The point-mapping derivation is useful and the composition domain is handled correctly. The current task emphasizes horizontal translation, while the advertised formula has four transformation parameters.
entries.change: Work through input and output transformations separately, then combine them. Include negative horizontal/vertical scales, the b=0 exceptional case, and both orders of a composition with different domains.
entries.interaction: Use guided controls for a, b, h and k, paired with an input→intermediate→output diagram. Keep the old and new graph points linked.
entries.check: Predict the transformed point and determine the composition domain before seeing either graph.

entries.title: Approach a point
entries.assessment: The removable-hole example and two-sided criterion are appropriate. They do not provide enough contrast to distinguish a limit, a point value, a jump and oscillation.
entries.change: Add a side-by-side classification of a removable hole, unequal one-sided limits, infinite behavior and oscillatory failure. Work a secant/velocity motivation with units instead of only mentioning it.
entries.interaction: Let the learner change f(a) without changing nearby values, and approach independently from either side. Label the excluded input explicitly.
entries.check: Explain why changing one point can repair continuity only when the surrounding limit already exists.

entries.title: Vertical asymptotes
entries.assessment: The 1/x and 1/x² comparison and M–δ argument are sound. The positive-cutoff experiment does not fully expose side-dependent signs or distinguish unboundedness from a limit to infinity.
entries.change: Add sign analysis on both sides, a removable-denominator-zero example, and an unbounded oscillatory example. State the quantifiers for positive and negative infinite limits.
entries.interaction: Give separate left/right approaches and a selectable height threshold M. Distinguish clipped graph values from mathematical infinity.
entries.check: Prove one infinite limit and produce a counterexample to 'denominator zero implies vertical asymptote.'

entries.title: Limit laws and squeezing
entries.assessment: This card carries a large collection of source references and techniques. The selected squeeze example cannot replace instruction in limit algebra, rationalization, restrictions and the foundational trigonometric limit.
entries.change: Split algebraic evaluation from squeeze proofs. Derive sin(x)/x→1 geometrically in radians without relying on the derivative it will later justify; include rationalization and nonzero-denominator hypotheses.
entries.interaction: Allow selection of competing bounds and display why each inequality holds, not just whether two plotted curves appear close.
entries.check: Choose a valid method for a new limit and give an all-nearby-input justification.

entries.title: Make “close” precise
entries.assessment: The quantifier order and δ=min(1,ε/3) example are strong starts. An automatically supplied δ illustrates a proof but does not teach the learner to construct one.
entries.change: Separate scratchwork from the final quantified proof. Explain each restriction in the minimum, the negation of the definition, and why δ cannot depend on the tested x.
entries.interaction: Introduce an ε challenge, a learner-selected δ and an adversarial input. Finite tests should be labelled exploratory; the concluding inequality must certify the entire interval.
entries.check: Construct a correct δ for a nonlinear example and diagnose an invalid quantifier order.

entries.title: Continuity and intermediate values
entries.assessment: Continuity, extension and IVT are grouped together, while the bisection explanation relies on a completeness fact that is not developed here. Existence-versus-uniqueness is correctly cautioned.
entries.change: Give the three continuity checks, a piecewise matching example, a full IVT application and a failed-hypothesis example. Explain the nested-interval/completeness step if calling the bisection argument a proof.
entries.interaction: Contrast a continuous crossing with a jump across the same target height; make endpoint values and target assumptions visible together.
entries.check: Use IVT to prove existence without claiming uniqueness, and explain exactly why it cannot be used for a discontinuous example.

entries.title: From secants to a tangent
entries.assessment: The quadratic difference-quotient derivation is a good anchor. It needs a clearer transition from a derivative at one input to the derivative function and from parameter change to physical rate.
entries.change: Work the same derivative symbolically, geometrically and with units. Distinguish f, f′, f′(a), the tangent line and an average rate; show signed increments on both sides.
entries.interaction: Display the quotient and its simplified expression together. At h=0 show the limit value as a limit, not as evaluation of the original 0/0 expression.
entries.check: Derive a derivative from the definition and explain what each quantity on the screen represents.

entries.title: Where differentiability fails
entries.assessment: The absolute-value corner and differentiability⇒continuity proof are useful. Higher derivatives, acceleration, vertical tangents and other failure types need more than a shared card.
entries.change: Separate corners, vertical tangents and oscillatory derivative failure. Include a differentiable function with a discontinuous derivative, and develop second derivatives/acceleration as a short bridge.
entries.interaction: Compare one-sided secants for each failure type. Do not let a near-vertical finite mesh impersonate an infinite derivative.
entries.check: Distinguish continuity, finite differentiability and derivative continuity with explicit examples.

entries.title: Build derivatives from rules
entries.assessment: The product-rule derivation is worth retaining. One x sin(x) example and a generic tangent experiment do not teach the full power/product/quotient/trigonometric toolkit.
entries.change: Publish a complete, domain-aware rule table; derive representative rules and work combined expressions in annotated steps. Include the standard trigonometric derivatives and their dependence on radians.
entries.interaction: For the product rule, show the two separate contributions to the change of a product; match colored terms to their geometric roles.
entries.check: Differentiate a mixed expression, name each rule used and verify the domain of the result.

entries.title: The chain rule
entries.assessment: The local-expansion proof uses little-o notation before it has been adequately introduced in the learning sequence. A correct compact proof is not automatically an accessible first proof.
entries.change: Introduce the meaning of a first-order remainder before this proof, or provide an elementary route followed by an advanced proof. Work nested compositions and evaluation points explicitly.
entries.interaction: Link inner and outer graphs, input changes and their corresponding local scale factors. A dependency diagram should expose the multiplication of rates.
entries.check: Differentiate a three-layer composition and explain why each derivative is evaluated at its particular input.

entries.title: Implicit curves and related rates
entries.assessment: The circle example correctly connects a constraint with time derivatives, but two distinct skills are crowded together. Branch selection, word-problem modeling and units are underdeveloped.
entries.change: Separate implicit differentiation from related rates. Add a full ladder or cone problem: diagram, constraint, differentiation, substitution, signed rate and units. Explain where solving for y locally fails.
entries.interaction: Make a moving constrained configuration and show both its geometric equation and its time derivative. Provide a vertical-tangent branch-switch case.
entries.check: Translate a new verbal rate problem into a constraint and compute the requested rate without substituting constants too early.

entries.title: Linear approximation and differentials
entries.assessment: The exact quadratic remainder and dy versus Δy distinction are valuable. Learners need an actual numerical approximation and a clear separation between an estimate and a certified error bound.
entries.change: Define little-o and big-O at the level needed here. Work one numerical approximation and one measurement-error problem, with both absolute and relative errors.
entries.interaction: Show f, its affine model, signed residual and normalized residual at the same displacement. Separate first-order prediction from a rigorous error envelope.
entries.check: State when an approximation is useful, calculate it and justify any claimed error bound.

entries.title: Extrema and critical points
entries.assessment: The compact-interval example is appropriate, but a final maximum/minimum value is not a substitute for a complete candidate comparison. Endpoint and nondifferentiable candidates need equal prominence.
entries.change: Show the critical-point calculation, endpoint list and value table in full. Include |x|, an open interval and an unbounded domain to distinguish existence from candidate finding.
entries.interaction: Link candidate markers to a comparison table and label local versus absolute extrema separately.
entries.check: Find every absolute extremum on a specified domain and justify that no candidate class was omitted.

entries.title: Rolle and the mean value theorem
entries.assessment: MVT is derived from Rolle, but Rolle's independent justification is not supplied here. Later L’Hôpital refers to Cauchy's MVT, which is another missing link.
entries.change: Prove Rolle using EVT and Fermat, derive MVT from it, and provide Cauchy's MVT as a linked lemma. Work derivative bounds, monotonicity and uniqueness-of-antiderivative consequences.
entries.interaction: Show the subtraction of the secant line and the resulting equal-endpoint function. Contrast a corner that defeats Rolle's hypotheses.
entries.check: Prove a nontrivial inequality using MVT and identify the exact interval hypotheses.

entries.title: Shape from derivatives
entries.assessment: Correction needed: the first-derivative sign-change test omits continuity at the candidate. The second-derivative regularity is also described vaguely, and the example should explicitly say local maximum/minimum.
entries.change: State continuity on an interval containing c and differentiability away from c for the first-derivative test. Give a precise sufficient second-derivative theorem. Include the discontinuous counterexample in Finding M1 and x³/x⁴ contrasts.
entries.interaction: Use coordinated f, f′ and f″ plots plus sign charts. Permit a point-value change to demonstrate why continuity at c matters.
entries.check: Apply both tests with their hypotheses and explain why f″(c)=0 proves neither an extremum nor an inflection.

entries.title: Infinity and curve sketching
entries.assessment: The slant-asymptote difference criterion and crossing caution are good. A single rational example does not teach the complete process of curve sketching or both directions of infinity.
entries.change: Work one rational function from domain and intercepts through asymptotes, derivative sign charts, concavity and a final sketch. Treat sqrt(x²)=|x| explicitly when comparing ±∞.
entries.interaction: Reveal graph features only after the learner predicts them; distinguish an off-screen branch from an asymptote.
entries.check: Construct and justify a sketch without using the plotted graph as the proof.

entries.title: Turn a constraint into an optimum
entries.assessment: The rectangle problem provides a clean first example but too little transfer. Learners need to formulate objectives and feasible sets themselves, not merely differentiate a provided quadratic.
entries.change: Add a shifted-axis geometry or cost problem with nontrivial domain restrictions, plus a noncompact example where a supremum is not attained. Explain the role of boundary degeneracies.
entries.interaction: Tie the geometric configuration to a feasible-domain interval and objective graph. Reject geometrically impossible parameter values.
entries.check: Solve a new optimization problem from words through a global conclusion, including units and feasibility.

entries.title: Newton’s tangent iteration
entries.assessment: The square-root example and convergence caveats are correct, but moving a starting point is not the same as understanding a sequence of iterates.
entries.change: Add an iteration table, stopping criteria, residual-versus-root-error distinction, and a precise local convergence statement at an appropriate level. Include the 0↔1 cycle for x³−2x+2.
entries.interaction: Provide explicit next-step controls, iteration history and failure states for zero/small derivatives, cycles and escape.
entries.check: Explain why a small residual or one plausible tangent step is not a general convergence certificate.

entries.title: Recover a function from its rate
entries.assessment: Constants on connected intervals are handled carefully. The same basic family is repeated in MH1101; this instance should prepare a genuine application rather than duplicate a reference card.
entries.change: Develop velocity→position with an initial condition and piecewise time intervals. Distinguish displacement from distance and explain componentwise constants on disconnected domains.
entries.interaction: Link the rate graph, accumulated change and selectable initial value. Changing the constant should translate position without altering velocity.
entries.check: Reconstruct motion from a rate and initial condition, with the correct interpretation of signed change.

entries.title: Invert a function
entries.assessment: Domain restriction and reciprocal slopes are introduced, but differentiating f(f⁻¹(y))=y only derives the formula after inverse differentiability is justified. Inverse-trigonometric foundations are thin upstream of integration.
entries.change: State a sufficient inverse-function theorem before the formula derivation. Develop principal branches and domains/ranges for inverse trig functions, and distinguish inverse functions from reciprocals.
entries.interaction: Link a function, its inverse, y=x and corresponding tangent points. Include x² on an unrestricted and then restricted domain.
entries.check: Choose a valid inverse branch and use the inverse derivative theorem with its hypotheses.

entries.title: Exponential and logarithmic rates
entries.assessment: The x^x example is useful. The natural exponential's defining property, logarithm laws and their logical foundation deserve a more explicit route rather than mutually supporting assertions.
entries.change: State how exp/log are being introduced and which facts are assumed or proved. Add logarithmic differentiation of a product/quotient, growth comparisons and domain checks.
entries.interaction: Link exponential growth, tangent slope and inverse logarithmic behavior; make forbidden logarithm inputs visible.
entries.check: Differentiate a variable-power expression while preserving its real domain and explaining every logarithmic transformation.

entries.title: Indeterminate forms and L’Hôpital
entries.assessment: The eligibility conditions are considerably better than a rule-only summary. However, one easy 0/0 example does not cover the listed forms, and Cauchy's MVT is invoked without a developed prerequisite.
entries.change: State a precise one-sided theorem, supply the Cauchy-MVT bridge, and work ∞/∞ plus product, difference and variable-power conversions. Recheck conditions after each application.
entries.interaction: Use a method-choice exercise with eligible, convertible and ineligible limits; compare the original quotient with the derivative quotient without implying an algebraic identity.
entries.check: Explain why the rule applies, transform an indeterminate form correctly and recognize an inconclusive derivative-ratio limit.

entries.title: Antiderivatives form a family
entries.assessment: This is a sound recap of the preceding course, including the interval qualification. Repeating the same elementary family does not itself create progression.
entries.change: Make it a diagnostic bridge: recover the rule, identify the role of C, and move to initial-value and piecewise examples. Allow prepared learners to skip the recap.
entries.interaction: Couple derivative and antiderivative views with an initial-value selector, not only a vertical-shift slider.
entries.check: Distinguish the family of antiderivatives from a definite integral and select the correct member from data.

entries.title: Accumulate with Riemann sums
entries.assessment: The definition correctly demands sampling independence, and the quadratic sums are useful. Uniform partitions and one sampling choice dominate the actual worked experience.
entries.change: Write the general partition formula with Δx_i and mesh norm. Develop upper/lower sums, signed accumulation, linearity, additivity and comparison as distinct results with examples.
entries.interaction: Switch left/right/midpoint/arbitrary samples and uneven partitions, with negative heights included. Show upper/lower enclosure when available.
entries.check: Explain why convergence of one displayed sequence of sums is weaker than Riemann integrability.

entries.title: The average value of a function
entries.assessment: The equal-area idea and continuity-for-attainment distinction are mathematically good. The learner needs the complete evaluation and a counterexample when continuity is dropped.
entries.change: Work the x² average and its attaining point step by step, attach units, and contrast endpoint averaging with integral averaging. Include an integrable step function whose average is not attained.
entries.interaction: Display the signed equal-area rectangle and allow a noncontinuous example; do not label a missing intersection as a plotting failure.
entries.check: Compute an average and say whether a theorem guarantees that some input attains it.

entries.title: Differentiation meets accumulation
entries.assessment: Both FTC directions and the short-interval-average proof are present, but variable bounds are relegated to a caution. The central relation deserves a full instructional sequence.
entries.change: Separate FTC1 and FTC2, with assumptions and examples. Add negative integrands, net change, a moving lower bound and two variable endpoints; derive the chain-rule factors.
entries.interaction: Link the integrand, accumulated integral and the accumulation function's tangent. Highlight exactly which strips are added or removed.
entries.check: Differentiate an integral with two moving bounds and explain its sign and chain-rule factors geometrically.

entries.title: Substitution changes the variable
entries.assessment: The nonmonotone signed-substitution caveat is a strength. Unfortunately, the example maps 0 and 1 to 0 and 1, hiding the very endpoint change beginners need to learn.
entries.change: Use an example with visibly different transformed bounds, followed by an indefinite integral and a nonmonotone signed example. Account for every old variable and differential.
entries.interaction: Display old and new intervals and linked small increments, with orientation changes separated from unsigned geometric area.
entries.check: Transform bounds and integrand correctly without mixing old and new variables.

entries.title: Improper integrals are limits
entries.assessment: Endpoint splitting and the distinction from symmetric cancellation are already explained correctly. The treatment needs worked limits and comparison practice, not merely more warnings.
entries.change: Work an interior singularity, two independent infinite tails and both power thresholds. Contrast the ordinary improper integral of 1/x across zero with its symmetric principal-value calculation.
entries.interaction: Show two independent cutoffs; never force symmetric cancellation as the only experiment. Display each limit separately.
entries.check: Decide convergence only after checking every improper part and distinguish a principal value from an ordinary integral.

entries.title: Area between curves
entries.assessment: The x versus x² example is a useful starting point but avoids switching order and splitting at crossings.
entries.change: Work vertical and horizontal slicing of the same region, followed by a crossing that changes upper/lower order and a case needing multiple pieces.
entries.interaction: Let the learner select slice orientation and endpoints. Highlight overlaps or omitted regions caused by proposed bounds.
entries.check: Derive an area integral from a diagram and justify every split and subtraction order.

entries.title: Volumes from cross-sections
entries.assessment: The washer formula is present but the worked example is only a disk. General cross-sections and nonzero inner radii are not actually practiced.
entries.change: Add a real washer example, a shifted rotation axis and a noncircular cross-section problem. Derive radii as distances before squaring them.
entries.interaction: Link the planar generating region, the rotated solid and a labeled perpendicular cross-section. A 2D area plot alone is insufficient for the central spatial claim.
entries.check: Write the cross-sectional area correctly for a new axis and distinguish π(R²−r²) from π(R−r)².

entries.title: Volumes from cylindrical shells
entries.assessment: The thin-annulus derivation is a strength. Comparing the current shell and disk examples does not compare two methods on one solid, because their axes differ.
entries.change: Solve the same solid by shells and washers, including a case where one method is clearly simpler. Explain coverage and overlap when a region crosses the axis.
entries.interaction: Show a shell unwrapping into circumference×height×thickness and label the geometric radius.
entries.check: Choose a method, derive its bounds and independently check the result using the other method on the same solid.

entries.title: Integration by parts
entries.assessment: The product-rule derivation and xe^x example are correct, but repeated and cyclic integration appear largely as promises.
entries.change: Add ∫ln x, a repeated-parts polynomial–exponential example, a cyclic exponential–trigonometric example, and definite boundary terms. Explain why a choice makes progress.
entries.interaction: Track the boundary contribution and remaining integral as linked quantities; use an algebraic stepper for factor selection rather than a generic area slider.
entries.check: Choose u and dv deliberately and solve a problem that requires more than one application.

entries.title: Trigonometric integrals
entries.assessment: The odd-sine-power example is useful, but the task's sin² accumulation does not teach that substitution mechanism. Tangent–secant cases are too compressed.
entries.change: Give a parity-based strategy with worked sine/cosine and tangent/secant cases, including both-even powers and complete back-substitution.
entries.interaction: Highlight the reserved differential factor and the identity applied to the remaining power. Match the visual example to the algebraic case being taught.
entries.check: Select and justify an identity/substitution for a trigonometric product without relying on a memorized single example.

entries.title: Substitute a triangle
entries.assessment: The absolute-value issue and sign-restricted interval are handled well. Only the easiest arcsine integral is worked, and prerequisite inverse-trigonometric material needs strengthening.
entries.change: Work all three radical patterns, including completing the square and a nontrivial back-substitution. Show how the selected parameter interval fixes signs and injectivity.
entries.interaction: Couple the triangle to the algebra, labeling signed quantities and branch restrictions instead of silently deleting absolute values.
entries.check: Perform a substitution, choose a valid branch and return an answer in the original variable with its domain.

entries.title: Split a rational function
entries.assessment: The text names polynomial division, repeated factors and irreducible quadratics, but only a two-linear-factor decomposition is demonstrated. This is a major skill-coverage gap.
entries.change: Provide separate full examples of an improper fraction, repeated linear factors and irreducible quadratic factors. Solve the coefficient equations and integrate every resulting term.
entries.interaction: Use a decomposition builder that detects missing powers and numerators of the wrong degree; connect the sum of pieces with the original rational function.
entries.check: Construct the full decomposition form before solving coefficients and retain all denominator exclusions.

entries.title: Midpoint and trapezoidal rules
entries.assessment: Error constants and the quadratic example are correct, but the actual weighted-sum algorithms and how to find K need explicit instruction.
entries.change: State both numerical formulas with indexing, derive the basic error scaling and solve for a sufficient n from a requested tolerance. Include a nonpolynomial example and explain why two close answers do not certify error.
entries.interaction: Link the sample table, shapes, estimates and a proven error enclosure. Distinguish actual error in a known example from an a priori bound.
entries.check: Choose a valid derivative bound and a subdivision count that certifies a prescribed accuracy.

entries.title: Simpson’s parabolic rule
entries.assessment: The weights, even-n requirement and quartic error example are good. The theorem's smoothness condition should be explicit instead of 'usual assumptions.'
entries.change: State a clear C⁴ sufficient version, derive one panel's weights and explain cubic exactness. Compare evaluation cost and guaranteed accuracy with midpoint/trapezoid methods.
entries.interaction: Show paired panels and their interpolating parabolas, reject odd n with an explanation, and display a real error budget.
entries.check: Apply the correct weights and justify the number of panels needed for a tolerance.

entries.title: Sequences and their limits
entries.assessment: The ε–N definition and tail emphasis are sound. Extending a finite plot is not a learner-generated tail argument.
entries.change: Add explicit N construction, divergent-to-infinity versus nonconvergent oscillation, and exercises requiring control of every late term.
entries.interaction: Let the learner set ε and propose N; separate a finite diagnostic search from the symbolic tail inequality.
entries.check: Produce an N(ε) proof and explain why a long apparently stable plot is not sufficient.

entries.title: Subsequences expose divergence
entries.assessment: The even/odd example and boundedness proof are appropriate. The lesson needs cases beyond constant subsequences and clearer implication logic.
entries.change: Include an oscillatory sequence with nonconstant convergent subsequences, the failure of bounded⇒convergent, and a sequence with successive differences→0 that still diverges. Label Bolzano–Weierstrass as an additional theorem if introduced.
entries.interaction: Select subsequences and compare their limiting bands; prohibit repeating a fixed index as a false subsequence.
entries.check: Disprove convergence by two valid subsequences and distinguish necessary conditions from sufficient ones.

entries.title: Calculate sequence limits
entries.assessment: The real-extension caveat for L’Hôpital is valuable. One rational limit and the shared sequence scene do not cover the full toolbox.
entries.change: Add rationalization, squeezing, dominant powers, root-type limits and all geometric-ratio cases, including r<−1. Explain the one-way restriction from a real function limit to integer inputs.
entries.interaction: Compare a sequence with two different continuous-domain extensions to expose why the converse fails.
entries.check: Choose a legal sequence-limit method and justify any passage to a real-variable extension.

entries.title: Monotone and bounded
entries.assessment: The supremum proof is good but presupposes completeness. Recursive sequences are advertised, yet the worked example is the explicit sequence 1−2⁻ⁿ.
entries.change: Explain least upper bounds, then work a recurrence such as a_(n+1)=sqrt(2+a_n): prove a bound and monotonicity before solving the fixed-point equation.
entries.interaction: Link recursive steps to an invariant interval and a cobweb or term plot; mark the difference between a candidate limit and proved convergence.
entries.check: Complete an induction-based recurrence proof in the correct logical order.

entries.title: A series is a sequence of sums
entries.assessment: The finite geometric identity and telescoping example are valuable. The distinction between term sequence and partial-sum sequence should be made impossible to miss.
entries.change: Add shifted indexing, nonunit first terms and negative geometric ratios. Work telescoping with its finite boundary terms fully written before taking a limit.
entries.interaction: Display a_n and S_n in separate linked panels and animate exact cancellation for telescoping rather than reuse only the geometric scene.
entries.check: Derive a finite partial sum and only then determine convergence and its sum.

entries.title: The term test only rules out
entries.assessment: The harmonic block proof is a strong piece of content. It should become the entry point to a method-selection system, rather than remain one isolated caution.
entries.change: Develop the implication and its contrapositive explicitly. Include finite initial changes and examples where term limits exist, fail or are zero but inconclusive.
entries.interaction: Show harmonic blocks contributing a fixed lower amount while individual terms shrink, alongside a convergent comparison.
entries.check: State exactly what the term test concludes and never infer convergence from a_n→0.

entries.title: Compare a series with an area
entries.assessment: The hypotheses and tail bounds are correct. The learner needs practice verifying eventual decrease and turning a remainder bound into a numerical guarantee.
entries.change: Work a logarithmic benchmark and a target-accuracy calculation, checking positivity, continuity and monotonicity on the appropriate tail.
entries.interaction: Link rectangles with upper/lower tail integrals, and show separately the partial sum and the bounded remaining amount.
entries.check: Apply the test with verified hypotheses and choose N to bound the remaining series error.

entries.title: Direct and limit comparison
entries.assessment: The inequality directions and 0/∞ ratio caveat are good. The 1/(n²+1) example is too forgiving to teach benchmark selection.
entries.change: Add a divergence comparison, a mixed polynomial/logarithmic example, and one-way ratio limits. Explain how dominant terms suggest a comparison and how to turn that suggestion into an inequality.
entries.interaction: Ask the learner to choose a benchmark and inequality direction before revealing a proof.
entries.check: Classify an unfamiliar positive series and justify the comparison in the correct direction.

entries.title: Absolute and conditional convergence
entries.assessment: The alternating test, remainder bound and conditional harmonic example are good. The equality to ln 2 is stated before its derivation is connected to later material.
entries.change: Separate the proof of absolute⇒ordinary convergence from the alternating proof. Add error signs, tolerance selection and a failed-monotonicity example. Link a valid later derivation of the ln 2 value.
entries.interaction: Display even/odd enclosures and the next-term error bound. Distinguish convergence classification from exact sum evaluation.
entries.check: Decide absolute/conditional/divergent status and give a justified signed approximation error.

entries.title: Ratio and root tests
entries.assessment: The factorial example and L=1 contrast are effective, but there is no comparably developed root-test example.
entries.change: Add an nth-power sequence where the root test is natural, an eventually undefined ratio with zeros, and an explicit inconclusive branch in the test-selection guide.
entries.interaction: Compare geometric envelopes with actual terms; require a q<1 bound rather than treating a finite ratio as the limiting ratio.
entries.check: Choose between ratio/root/comparison tests and explain why L=1 is not a verdict.

entries.title: Power series and their radius
entries.assessment: Correct the phrase 'a polynomial with infinitely many terms': a polynomial is finite. The convergence-radius discussion is otherwise careful, but the only endpoint example has both endpoints fail.
entries.change: Define a power series as a series of monomials and its sum where it converges. Work finite positive radius, radius zero/infinity and an interval with different endpoint behavior.
entries.interaction: Mark center, open convergence interval and separately tested endpoints. Keep partial polynomials distinct from the infinite sum.
entries.check: Find a radius and then independently classify both endpoints with an appropriate series test.

entries.title: Differentiate and integrate a series
entries.assessment: The smaller-interval uniform-control idea is good. The unchanged geometric-series experiment does not show how differentiation/integration alters coefficients or endpoint behavior.
entries.change: Derive the transformed series explicitly, state the same-radius theorem, and compare endpoint tests before/after an operation. Explain which interchange theorem is being used.
entries.interaction: Show original, differentiated and integrated partial sums with linked coefficients and independently labeled endpoint statuses.
entries.check: Generate a new representation and justify its domain without assuming endpoint behavior is preserved.

entries.title: Taylor polynomials and remainder
entries.assessment: The distinction between smoothness and equality to a Taylor series is already present; preserve it. One exponential example is insufficient practice in constructing coefficients and certifying accuracy.
entries.change: Derive coefficients, work a nonzero center, solve for the degree required by a tolerance, and develop a flat smooth/nonanalytic counterexample in an optional rigorous panel.
entries.interaction: Link derivatives at the center, partial polynomials, the actual function and a proven remainder envelope; do not imply universal improvement at every x.
entries.check: Separate a finite approximation guarantee from proof that an infinite Taylor series represents the function.

entries.title: The general binomial series
entries.assessment: The generalized coefficients and terminating-integer distinction are good. The square-root approximation needs normalization and error reasoning to become a reusable method.
entries.change: Work sqrt(4+x) or another rescaled expression, derive coefficients systematically and explain the valid interval and any endpoint analysis. Provide a finite error estimate for the numerical example.
entries.interaction: Display the normalization step, center and interval before allowing higher-degree comparisons.
entries.check: Convert an expression into binomial-series form and state where its approximation is justified.

entries.title: Extract a limit from a series
entries.assessment: The leading-term reasoning and sufficient remainder order are sound. Big-O notation needs a prerequisite explanation and more varied order-selection problems.
entries.change: Add a short O/o guide, nested substitutions and cancellations requiring more terms. Explicitly distinguish a convergent power-series identity from a finite asymptotic expansion.
entries.interaction: Let the learner choose truncation order and show whether the remainder is small enough after division.
entries.check: Justify a series-based limit by controlling the normalized remainder, not only by canceling formal terms.

entries.title: Vectors in space
entries.assessment: The point/free-vector distinction, vector identities and geometric dot-product explanation are strong. Coordinates, norm, basis, angle and orthogonality still arrive in a dense cluster.
entries.change: Add worked nonunit-vector calculations, projections and Cauchy–Schwarz before using them downstream. Distinguish zero-vector algebraic orthogonality from an angle between nonzero vectors.
entries.interaction: Pair coordinate calculations with vector addition/projection and a length scale; allow magnitudes as well as angle to change.
entries.check: Translate between a geometric displacement and coordinates, compute a projection and justify an angle calculation.

entries.title: A curve and its clock
entries.assessment: The distinction between image, traversal and singular clock is unusually good. The onto-map and Peano-curve remarks need pacing so they clarify rather than obscure first exposure.
entries.change: Separate arbitrary reparametrizations from regular monotone changes of parameter. Work the same path with different speeds, reversed orientation and repeated traversal; move space-filling curves into supported enrichment.
entries.interaction: Synchronize two traversals of the same curve with independently controlled clocks and a shared point correspondence.
entries.check: Explain which changes preserve the image, orientation, regularity and multiplicity, and which do not.

entries.title: Build a parametrization
entries.assessment: The cycloid derivation and two-way parameter elimination are valuable. Several other curve families are listed too quickly for learners to build parametrizations themselves.
entries.change: Provide one construction per family, emphasizing the parameter interval. Add a non-affine line parametrization and a task where elimination introduces extra points unless the range is checked.
entries.interaction: Retain the available family selector and make each family reveal its generating geometry, especially the rolling circle for the cycloid.
entries.check: Construct a parametrization from a geometric description and verify its exact image in both directions.

entries.title: Tangents, velocity and singularities
entries.assessment: The cusp versus zero-velocity distinction is mathematically careful. A helix example does not visually establish all claims about self-intersections, singularities and one-sided tangents.
entries.change: Develop vector difference quotients, tangent lines, speed and acceleration separately. Add a regular line with a singular clock, a cusp, a crossing with two visits and a one-sided endpoint.
entries.interaction: Make the secant vector approach a tangent and distinguish velocity magnitude from geometric tangent direction. Use the actual contrasting curves.
entries.check: Decide whether a vanishing velocity reflects a coordinate failure or a geometric singularity, with a justified tangent analysis.

entries.title: Surfaces and level sets
entries.assessment: The graph-versus-domain-level-set distinction and domain examples are correct. The present paraboloid is too special to establish intuition about arbitrary contours and nongraph surfaces.
entries.change: Add saddle, disconnected-level-set, empty-level-set and critical-level examples, plus explicit domain inequalities. Explain what topographic contour spacing measures locally.
entries.interaction: Couple the 3D graph to a true 2D contour plot and horizontal slice, with the selected c synchronized across all three.
entries.check: Recover a level-set equation and distinguish its position in the input plane from the lifted graph intersection.

entries.title: Distance and neighborhoods
entries.assessment: The metric axioms and ambient-space caveat are good. Open/closed/limit/isolated/boundary ideas need concrete contrasts rather than a single moving disk probe.
entries.change: Add a small notation/logic lesson and examples that are open only, closed only, neither and both. Distinguish closure, boundary, interior and accumulation points; state any completeness facts needed later.
entries.interaction: Let the learner choose a point and radius and classify the relevant neighborhood condition on different sets.
entries.check: Explain why membership alone does not imply being a limit point and prove an open/closed classification.

entries.title: The ε–δ limit
entries.assessment: The full quantifier statement and radial proof are strong. The automatically selected radius does not teach construction, and the vector example introduces substantial unrelated single-variable calculations.
entries.change: Build from a scalar radial bound to vector component bounds, proving uniqueness and explaining permitted-domain limit points. Add a full learner-produced δ argument and its negation.
entries.interaction: Use independent ε, proposed δ and input controls, with an algebraic certificate covering all points in the disk rather than only sampled directions.
entries.check: Prove a multivariable limit using an explicit uniform neighborhood estimate.

entries.title: Why a limit does not exist
entries.assessment: The axes-versus-diagonal example is correct and well chosen. It should be tied more explicitly to the restriction theorem and to the asymmetry between proving and disproving existence.
entries.change: State and derive the restriction lemma. Add a restriction with oscillation and clarify when paths lie in the permitted domain and really approach the target.
entries.interaction: Display two simultaneous approach paths, their lifted values and the same shrinking radius. Preserve the domain hole.
entries.check: Disprove a limit using valid paths while explaining why agreement on chosen paths would not prove it.

entries.title: All lines can be misleading
entries.assessment: This is one of the strongest conceptual examples: all line limits agree while parabolic paths disagree. Its denominator-balancing strategy should become an explicit problem-solving method.
entries.change: Derive the choice y=kx² from the competing denominator scales. Explain why fixed-angle polar limits are still line tests and what uniformity in angle would require.
entries.interaction: Compare fixed lines with the whole parabolic family and a radius-dependent angle. Display the persistent discrepancy rather than only a decorative surface.
entries.check: Discover a curved obstruction for a new rational expression and explain why every-line testing was insufficient.

entries.title: Squeeze, extend, compose
entries.assessment: The radial bounds and isolated-point caveat are correct. Several algebraic limit laws, continuity operations and extension ideas are compressed into one card.
entries.change: Work one complete ε–δ proof from the bound, then separately develop extension, quotient-domain conditions, componentwise continuity and composition.
entries.interaction: Show the bound as an enclosing error envelope for every angle and let the learner choose the extension value at the missing point.
entries.check: Find a useful radial estimate and determine the unique continuous extension when one exists.

entries.title: Infinity means every escape route
entries.assessment: The distinction between norm-infinity and iterated positive-coordinate limits is valuable. Learners need an explicit comparison of the different domains and quantifiers.
entries.change: State the all-outside-a-ball definition, contrast it with limits in a quadrant, and add escape paths with changing direction. Work the reciprocal-radius estimate completely.
entries.interaction: Couple an expanding excluded ball to a bound on all remaining values, rather than showing only one escaping point.
entries.check: Prove a norm-infinity limit or refute it with a permitted escape path.

entries.title: Partial derivatives are slice slopes
entries.assessment: The use of the actual piecewise definition at the origin is excellent. The fixed-x paraboloid demo underserves two independent partial derivatives and derivative-domain questions.
entries.change: Work both coordinate difference quotients, a piecewise junction and a partial-derivative domain. Distinguish the two lifted tangent vectors from a justified tangent plane.
entries.interaction: Allow both slice coordinates to vary and compare axis restrictions with a nearby non-axis path.
entries.check: Compute partials at a junction directly and explain why their existence does not prove continuity or differentiability.

entries.title: Cross products build normal vectors
entries.assessment: The coordinate formula, nonparallel requirement and nonassociativity example are sound. Determinant area, orientation and the equivalence of plane descriptions deserve slower development.
entries.change: Derive the area magnitude and right-hand sign, then convert between normal, point-direction and Cartesian plane equations. Link the scalar triple product needed later.
entries.interaction: Reverse vector order and show the normal sign changing while the plane and unsigned area stay fixed.
entries.check: Build a plane from two independent directions and verify its normal by two dot products.

entries.title: What total differentiability means
entries.assessment: The affine-versus-linear distinction, uniqueness argument and normalized quadratic remainder are strong. The derivative as a linear map and little-o notation still need an explicit prerequisite bridge.
entries.change: Introduce the typed map Df(p), the affine approximation and o(‖h‖) in plain mathematical language. Expand the quadratic example into a complete quantified proof.
entries.interaction: Couple graph/plane comparison to raw residual and residual divided by distance across all directions. Do not rely only on surfaces looking close.
entries.check: Identify the only possible derivative and prove a uniform normalized-remainder estimate.

entries.title: All directional derivatives can exist—and still fail
entries.assessment: This lesson correctly refutes a major misconception with x³/(x²+y²), including a nonzero normalized diagonal remainder. It should be a central checkpoint, not an easily skipped subtlety.
entries.change: Organize an implication diagram for continuity, partials, directional derivatives and total differentiability. Explain both failures: nonlinear directional response and lack of a uniform remainder.
entries.interaction: Keep actual directional response and candidate-plane response visible together, with an exact counterexample direction.
entries.check: Explain why all directional derivatives existing does not supply a single linear derivative map.

entries.title: Certify the approximation
entries.assessment: The neighborhood hypothesis is carefully stated, and the cone-volume example explicitly distinguishes an estimate from a rigorous bound. The proof's two increments need to be expanded.
entries.change: Write the horizontal/vertical increment decomposition line by line and justify the intermediate-point limits. Develop a genuine finite remainder bound for the measurement-error example.
entries.interaction: Pair first-order error estimates with actual error and a certified envelope, so 'approximately' cannot be mistaken for 'at most.'
entries.check: Prove differentiability by a sufficient criterion and separately certify a requested numerical error bound.

entries.title: The chain rule as a composition of motions
entries.assessment: The derivative-matrix formulation is correct, but matrices and their dimensions arrive before a dedicated derivative-matrix foundation. A path of constant height makes all contributions cancel and is too special alone.
entries.change: Introduce Jacobian matrices as linear maps before using their product. Work a nonconstant-height path and a multi-input dependency tree, including evaluation at the intermediate point.
entries.interaction: Display each contribution to the total derivative separately before summing; link paths in the dependency tree to matrix entries.
entries.check: Multiply correctly shaped derivatives and explain every evaluation point in a multistage composition.

entries.title: Implicit surfaces become local graphs
entries.assessment: The theorem's regularity conditions are clear, and the text honestly says existence is not proved here. Learners still need to see why a coordinate choice can fail without the surface failing.
entries.change: Work the sphere near a pole and equator, switching the solved-for coordinate when necessary. Separate theorem-supplied existence from chain-rule derivation of the partial formulas.
entries.interaction: Show which projection is locally one-to-one and mark F_z=0 independently of ∇F=0.
entries.check: Choose a valid local graph coordinate and distinguish projection failure from a singular level set.

entries.title: Direction changes the slope
entries.assessment: The distinction between a defining directional limit and the gradient formula is correctly made. Normalization should become an active decision rather than a warning.
entries.change: Work a nonunit direction fully, state units per distance versus per parameter and reconnect to the nondifferentiable counterexample.
entries.interaction: Display the direction vector's norm and compare normalized and unnormalized rates. Provide a link to the failure of the gradient shortcut.
entries.check: Compute a directional derivative by a justified method and explain when normalization is required.

entries.title: The gradient points uphill and across contours
entries.assessment: The nonzero-gradient and regular-level-set conditions are good. Cauchy–Schwarz, the equality condition and input-space versus graph-space arrows need explicit support.
entries.change: Prove the maximization over unit directions, handle ∇f=0 separately and derive orthogonality along level curves. Distinguish the gradient in the domain from the graph's normal in three dimensions.
entries.interaction: Link a 2D contour map and gradient arrow to the 3D graph; label the lifted tangent direction separately from the surface normal.
entries.check: Identify steepest first-order increase and explain why it is neither a guaranteed global optimization path nor the graph's normal vector.

entries.title: Stationary does not mean optimal
entries.assessment: The parameter family and broader course convention for critical points are explained well. Learners need a precise distinction between strict and non-strict extrema and between stationary and nondifferentiable candidates.
entries.change: Give explicit definitions relative to the domain, include a boundary extremum and a nondifferentiable minimum, and tie each classification to inequalities rather than appearance.
entries.interaction: Show directional slices and their signs as the quadratic parameter crosses zero, including the entire line of non-strict minima.
entries.check: Classify a candidate using its definition and identify points omitted by solving only ∇f=0.

entries.title: Second derivatives and changing slopes
entries.assessment: The derivative-order convention and Clairaut hypothesis are commendably explicit. The rectangular-increment proof is too compressed and no failed-regularity example is developed.
entries.change: Expand the double mean-value argument, work higher mixed notation, and add a standard example with unequal mixed partials at a point.
entries.interaction: Visualize the rectangular increment as four signed function values, with the two differentiation orders tracked separately.
entries.check: Compute mixed partials using the stated convention and know when exchanging order is justified.

entries.title: Classify the second-order shape
entries.assessment: This is mathematically rich: degenerate examples, nonisolated critical sets and local/global distinctions are already present. The gap is scaffolding quadratic forms, eigenvalues and domination of the remainder.
entries.change: Explain definiteness and principal directions before the determinant shortcut. Work a rotated quadratic with a nonzero mixed term and develop the degenerate comparison examples.
entries.interaction: Rotate into principal directions and connect the quadratic form's sign to the exact function near the point.
entries.check: Classify a stationary point with hypotheses checked and use another argument when the Hessian test is inconclusive.

entries.title: Global extrema require the boundary
entries.assessment: The rectangular example correctly examines all edges and the interior. It is dense enough that a learner can miss the bookkeeping and the role of existence.
entries.change: Turn the computation into a full candidate table, including corners, edge critical points and the interior point. Develop compactness versus noncompact inequalities as separate cases.
entries.interaction: Color each boundary restriction and link its candidates to the table; distinguish guaranteed attainment from a numerical search result.
entries.check: Produce an exhaustive candidate comparison and separately justify that a global extremum exists.

entries.title: Lagrange multipliers on a curve
entries.assessment: The feasible-tangent argument and warning about dividing away candidates are good. The example is too symmetric to teach robust equation solving by itself.
entries.change: Work all multiplier equations explicitly, then add a case with a zero coordinate and a singular constraint point requiring separate examination.
entries.interaction: Show feasible tangent, objective gradient and constraint gradient together; use candidate markers with a value comparison.
entries.check: Find and compare every admissible candidate without assuming the multiplier equations alone prove a maximum.

entries.title: One constraint in three dimensions
entries.assessment: The global Cauchy–Schwarz certificate is excellent. The open-top-box AM–GM argument is substantive instruction buried in a pitfall paragraph.
entries.change: Promote the box into a full worked application and explain the difference between a compact feasible set and a separate global inequality on a noncompact one.
entries.interaction: Keep the sphere as a spatial constraint rather than implying a 3-variable objective graph fits in 3D; show objective values by labels or a scalar scale.
entries.check: Solve a three-variable constraint problem and provide an independent argument that the candidate is globally optimal.

entries.title: Two constraints and one tangent direction
entries.assessment: The independence condition and counterexample with equal constraint gradients are mathematically strong. The row-space/kernel proof needs a linear-algebra bridge.
entries.change: Explain rank, kernel and normal span geometrically before the compact proof. Work the full system and a dependent-gradient failure separately.
entries.interaction: Display both normals, their cross product and the objective gradient's tangential component; show what happens when rank drops.
entries.check: Verify independence and explain why two nonzero normals are not enough.

entries.title: A double integral from columns
entries.assessment: Sampling independence and the exact midpoint error are well explained. Uniform continuity is doing important work without a developed prerequisite theorem.
entries.change: State and explain continuous-on-compact⇒uniformly-continuous, then expand the oscillation bound. Use nonuniform cells, independent subdivisions and signed integrands as well as the positive example.
entries.interaction: Let sample locations vary, compare upper/lower columns and display the error certificate separately from the finite visualization.
entries.check: Explain why every sufficiently fine sampling has the same limit, not merely why midpoint sums converge.

entries.title: Integrating a bounded region
entries.assessment: The zero-extension construction and Jordan/Lebesgue distinction are sophisticated and largely careful. They introduce more foundational machinery than the learning path currently supports.
entries.change: Define Jordan area and zero-area boundaries with explicit coverings. Separate the course's elementary sufficient condition from the more general Lebesgue discontinuity criterion, with a supported enrichment route.
entries.interaction: Link the region, its zero extension on a rectangle and a density/units interpretation; use an irregular boundary to explain why geometry matters.
entries.check: State the integration framework and justify area/mass/probability calculations without conflating Jordan and Lebesgue notions.

entries.title: Fubini: accumulate one direction at a time
entries.assessment: The finite-sum regrouping idea is good, but the symmetric example makes both orders equally easy and conceals why order choice matters.
entries.change: Add an asymmetric integrand where one order simplifies the problem. State separately the continuous-rectangle theorem and any broader version needed for zero extensions.
entries.interaction: Show an actual slice integral as a function of the remaining coordinate, not only columns viewed from different camera angles.
entries.check: Derive and evaluate both orders for one example and justify the theorem used.

entries.title: Type I and Type II regions
entries.assessment: The region definitions, bound-dependence warning and triangle calculation are good. The example requires no piecewise decomposition and makes reversal unusually easy.
entries.change: Work a curved region requiring a split in one order, including its projection and intersection calculations. Make explicit the Riemann-Fubini version used after zero extension, since that extension is generally discontinuous on the boundary.
entries.interaction: Link vertical/horizontal slices to editable bounds and shade the set those bounds actually describe.
entries.check: Reverse integration order by reconstructing the same region, including all required pieces.

entries.title: Linearity and cutting a region
entries.assessment: The distinction between algebraic linearity and geometric additivity is clear, with a useful overlap warning. It needs practice on a less trivial decomposition.
entries.change: Add inclusion–exclusion for positive-area overlap, a sign-changing integrand and a region that becomes simple only after splitting. Explain indicator notation before using it in the proof.
entries.interaction: Let the learner draw or choose a cut and show counted-once, omitted and double-counted areas.
entries.check: Decompose a region without altering its integral and explain why shared edges contribute zero in this setting.

entries.title: Polar coordinates and the area factor
entries.assessment: The exact annular-cell derivation is a strong foundation. The learner should see the parameter rectangle as well as its physical image and understand angular nonuniqueness.
entries.change: Work coordinate conversion with quadrants and derive the factor from both exact cells and the derivative matrix. Explain seams, r=0 and one-turn coverage.
entries.interaction: Show equal parameter cells at different radii side by side with their image cells and measured area ratios.
entries.check: Derive dA=r dr dθ rather than insert it from memory, and choose bounds that avoid repeated positive-area coverage.

entries.title: Variable polar bounds
entries.assessment: The text explicitly admits that the scene still displays a centered constant-radius sector. This is a central concept–experiment mismatch: the distinctive variable boundary is left to paper.
entries.change: Develop the shifted disk completely, then a region with inner/outer radial bounds or multiple radial intervals. Explain how the angle interval follows from nonnegative radii.
entries.interaction: Render the actual shifted disk and a moving ray with endpoints r=h₁(θ), h₂(θ). Keep its parameter-domain region visible.
entries.check: Derive variable polar bounds from a Cartesian inequality and verify exact coverage.

entries.title: A triple integral accumulates through space
entries.assessment: The distinction between a solid domain and a hypothetical 4D graph is important and correctly made. A horizontal slice alone does not show the three-dimensional sum definition.
entries.change: Add a density example with units and a voxel-sum construction before the slicing shortcut. State the compactness/uniform-continuity ingredients of convergence explicitly.
entries.interaction: Alternate between cells, the solid boundary and cross-sections; distinguish volume from mass when density changes.
entries.check: Explain what is being summed and why integrating 1 is different from integrating a nonconstant density.

entries.title: Type I, II and III solids
entries.assessment: All three descriptions are available, with careful projection hypotheses. The text should become a stepwise exercise in deriving nested bounds instead of a finished list to memorize.
entries.change: Work the complete projection/fiber process in two orders, then include a solid with disconnected fibers that must be split. Explain the course-specific naming convention.
entries.interaction: Show the chosen projection plane, one fiber and its two endpoints simultaneously; preview the region implied by proposed bounds.
entries.check: Reconstruct valid triple-integral bounds in a new order and verify that all radicals remain real throughout the outer domain.

entries.title: Cylindrical coordinates
entries.assessment: The radius-to-axis distinction and atan2/quadrant warning are good. The fixed cylinder/wedge does not fully teach coordinate surfaces and conversion.
entries.change: Add conversions in all quadrants, the axis singularity, constant-coordinate surfaces, a cone and an off-axis point.
entries.interaction: Let radius, azimuth and height vary independently with Cartesian and cylindrical coordinates displayed together.
entries.check: Translate between coordinate systems and recognize which geometric constraints cylindrical coordinates simplify.

entries.title: Cylindrical volume elements
entries.assessment: The derivation from vertical fibers plus polar area is coherent. The radial-density example correctly distinguishes the density factor from the Jacobian factor.
entries.change: Work a paraboloid-bounded solid or other nonconstant height example, deriving all bounds and checking a second method. Keep density, geometry and measure factors separately labeled.
entries.interaction: Show an actual small wedge and its three edge lengths, with a density control that leaves the solid unchanged.
entries.check: Transform the domain, density and volume element independently and explain every factor of r.

entries.title: Spherical coordinates
entries.assessment: Coordinate conventions and pole/origin nonuniqueness are carefully stated. A moving cap boundary does not give learners full control of a point's three coordinates.
entries.change: Add Cartesian↔spherical conversions and a table of constant-coordinate surfaces, including the equatorial special case. Explain the difference between a spherical surface cap and a solid sector.
entries.interaction: Provide independent ρ, θ and φ controls with a visible right-triangle decomposition and convention labels.
entries.check: Convert a point and a surface equation while using the stated inclination/azimuth convention consistently.

entries.title: Spherical wedges and radial bounds
entries.assessment: The volume factor and sector-versus-cap warning are good. The proof invokes change of variables before the general theorem is taught; this dependency should be explicit.
entries.change: Label the geometric derivation as motivation and link the later theorem, or reorder the proof. Work an off-center sphere or plane-cut cap with genuinely variable radial bounds.
entries.interaction: Show the radial interval for each direction and compare a sector reaching the origin with a cap that does not.
entries.check: Derive all three spherical bounds and distinguish ρ²sinφ as measure distortion from any density factor.

entries.title: A determinant scales area
entries.assessment: The interpolated determinant 1+2s is correctly distinguished from its final value 3. This is a useful anchor for local area change, but orientation reversal and collapse are only described.
entries.change: Add determinant-zero and negative-determinant maps, derive parallelogram area and make the input/output coordinate order explicit.
entries.interaction: Show the images of the basis vectors, area ratio and orientation throughout the deformation, including a reflection and a rank drop.
entries.check: Predict signed determinant and unsigned area scaling before calculating them.

entries.title: The Jacobian is a local determinant
entries.assessment: The matrix/determinant distinction and local-versus-global injectivity caveat are correct. The actual experiment is linear, so it cannot demonstrate spatially varying local distortion.
entries.change: Work a nonlinear map in full: derivative matrix at a point, determinant field and shrinking-cell limit. Contrast local invertibility with a map that overlaps globally.
entries.interaction: Use T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v) on 0≤u,v≤1 as a first nonlinear lab; compare equal cells at different u and then shrink one cell.
entries.check: Compute a local area factor and explain why a nonzero Jacobian does not imply global one-to-one behavior.

entries.title: Space transformations and signed Jacobians
entries.assessment: The negative spherical determinant for the order (ρ,θ,φ) is correctly handled—a detail many elementary treatments blur. The scalar triple-product and orientation argument needs a more direct visual derivation.
entries.change: Expand the determinant calculation and compare two column orders, a reflection and a rank-deficient map. Keep signed volume and ordinary volume distinct.
entries.interaction: Display the three derivative columns and their parallelepiped, with a coordinate-order switch that flips determinant sign without changing volume.
entries.check: Determine the sign from ordered derivative vectors and use the absolute value in ordinary triple integration.

entries.title: Change of variables in two and three dimensions
entries.assessment: The clean diffeomorphism theorem and multiplicity caveat are good. One linear parallelogram example does not prepare learners to choose a nonlinear substitution themselves.
entries.change: Add a full nonlinear boundary-straightening example, verify injectivity and regularity, and explain the permitted seam exceptions in standard coordinates. Label the proof as a sketch unless the approximation estimates are supplied.
entries.interaction: Synchronize parameter region, transformed region, integrand composition and local scale factor. Keep all three transformations visible.
entries.check: Derive a substitution from the boundary equations and verify domain, integrand and measure changes separately.

entries.title: When the substitution is given backwards
entries.assessment: The corresponding-point identity is careful and correct. A constant inverse determinant makes the evaluation-point issue almost invisible.
entries.change: Add a nonconstant example in which the reciprocal is evaluated at corresponding points, and connect it explicitly to the inverse function theorem and chain rule.
entries.interaction: Highlight a paired source/image point and its two reciprocal area factors; permit switching the direction of the map.
entries.check: Use a substitution given as u(x,y),v(x,y) without accidentally multiplying by the wrong determinant.

entries.title: A scalar field along a curve
entries.assessment: The ribbon interpretation and reparametrization invariance are good. Arc length and rectifiability need a more developed prerequisite than the short speed-factor derivation supplies.
entries.change: Add a dedicated arc-length bridge and a non-unit-speed example. Distinguish the image curve from repeated traversal and explain the meaning of linear density and units.
entries.interaction: Compare two clocks on the same curve, showing how speed and dt compensate; use a density that varies independently of the geometry.
entries.check: Compute ∫f ds with a non-unit-speed parametrization and explain why reversing orientation does not change it.

entries.title: Vector fields assign a direction at every point
entries.assessment: The distinction between field arrows and trajectories is excellent. The shared rotation field is too special to teach general local behavior or magnitude encoding.
entries.change: Add constant, shear, source/sink and singular fields. State whether arrow lengths are normalized, compressed or physically proportional, and separate field value from derivatives of the field.
entries.interaction: Provide a magnitude legend and exact vector readout at a selected point. Do not make a streamline or particle interpretation implicit.
entries.check: Evaluate a field and explain what its arrows do and do not say about a particle's motion.

entries.title: Work and orientation along a curve
entries.assessment: The signed dot-product derivation is correct. F exactly equal to the unit tangent makes the example unusually easy and hides negative and transverse contributions.
entries.change: Work a path where the dot product changes sign and a non-unit-speed parametrization, then compare a reversed and a repeated traversal.
entries.interaction: Add an actual reverse-orientation control and plot local F·r′ alongside accumulated work.
entries.check: Compute the signed integral and explain why force magnitude times path length is generally wrong.

entries.title: Three differentials, one path
entries.assessment: The course-specific meanings of first/second/third kinds and the ds distinction are explicitly clarified. The circle example should be expanded into a complete translation between notations.
entries.change: Work P dx+Q dy+R dz on a nonplanar path, deriving each differential and its sign. Explain the differential expression's dependence on orientation and parametrization.
entries.interaction: Show signed coordinate displacements and the three scalar contributions separately before summing them.
entries.check: Convert a coordinate line integral to a parameter integral without replacing dx,dy,dz by ds.

entries.title: Assemble a path from pieces
entries.assessment: Additivity and the special role of conservativeness are carefully distinguished. The scene is a parabola while the broken-path comparison is described algebraically.
entries.change: Work each segment of an actual polygonal path, including its own parameter interval and orientation. Add a nonconservative comparison so equal endpoints are not mistaken for general equality.
entries.interaction: Render and select each path piece, show its contribution and then the total; include a reversed piece as an error to diagnose.
entries.check: Parametrize and integrate a composite path with correct junctions and inherited orientation.

entries.title: Work is tangential accumulation
entries.assessment: This substantially repeats the earlier vector-line-integral example. The repetition should create new modeling skill rather than another unit-circle animation.
entries.change: Refocus on physical work, units, variable force and tangential/normal decomposition. Include a nonclosed trajectory and contrast work with arc length and total force magnitude.
entries.interaction: Show positive, zero and negative local work on the same path and a running signed integral.
entries.check: Translate a force-and-motion situation into a line integral and interpret the sign and units of its result.

entries.title: A potential remembers only endpoints
entries.assessment: The theorem's hypotheses and mechanics sign convention are particularly good. The chain-rule proof deserves a complete worked construction of a potential, not only use of one already supplied.
entries.change: Add potential recovery with coordinate-dependent integration constants, path independence and a direct calculation along two different paths. Preserve the point that simple connectedness is not required once a global potential is given.
entries.interaction: Let users deform a path with fixed endpoints and compare direct work with the potential difference.
entries.check: Find or verify a potential and justify an endpoint calculation on the entire path domain.

entries.title: When does zero curl suffice?
entries.assessment: The punctured-plane counterexample, loop condition and warning about Green's theorem are strong. Local potentials becoming a global potential is a substantial topological step needing support.
entries.change: Develop the potential/path-independence/zero-loop equivalences and give a guided potential-construction problem. Explain simple connectedness with loops, including why 'no holes' is imprecise in 3D.
entries.interaction: Retain the potential/vortex variants and visualize the excluded set, a contractible loop and a loop that cannot contract within the domain.
entries.check: Check the domain before using zero curl and explain the vortex's nonzero circulation without contradicting Green's theorem.

entries.title: Green’s Theorem
entries.assessment: The full-region smoothness and hole-orientation requirements are good. A disk circulation alone does not demonstrate cancellation of internal boundaries.
entries.change: Derive the rectangle case fully and state the extension argument's status. Work a multiply connected region and a failed interior-smoothness case.
entries.interaction: Add a tiled-region cancellation view, then expose only the surviving outer and inner boundaries with their correct arrows.
entries.check: Apply Green with the actual region, all boundary components and the correct orientation.

entries.title: Measure area from the boundary
entries.assessment: The three differential forms and ellipse calculation are useful. Self-intersection, signed multiplicity and the planimeter are mentioned but not taught as separate ideas.
entries.change: Work a polygon to derive the shoelace connection, develop orientation reversal and place self-intersecting curves in a supported signed-area extension.
entries.interaction: Trace a polygon or ellipse while accumulating x dy−y dx; make an orientation reversal change the sign, not the geometric region.
entries.check: Derive ordinary area from a valid positively oriented boundary and recognize when the integral instead measures signed multiplicity.

entries.title: A surface is a two-parameter image
entries.assessment: Seam versus geometric-edge and coordinate failure versus surface failure are handled well. Homeomorphism, chart interiors and boundary identifications need a preparatory explanation.
entries.change: Build from a graph patch to a sphere chart and then overlapping charts. Explain the course's parametrization convention without suggesting that one regular rectangular chart covers the whole sphere.
entries.interaction: Show the parameter domain and image side by side, with linked coordinate curves, seam identifications and a second chart at a pole.
entries.check: Distinguish a chart boundary from a genuine surface boundary and describe where a chosen chart is valid.

entries.title: Two tangents determine a normal
entries.assessment: The rank-two criterion and sphere-pole caveat are good. Using the sphere for every example hides nonorthogonal parameter tangents and genuine singularities.
entries.change: Add a sheared graph parametrization and compare a sphere's coordinate pole with a cone tip. Explain the derivative matrix's rank and tangent-plane equation.
entries.interaction: Display both parameter tangent vectors and their cross product, then switch charts without changing the geometric point.
entries.check: Decide whether a zero cross product indicates a bad chart or a geometric problem, with an appropriate replacement chart where possible.

entries.title: A tiny rectangle becomes a parallelogram
entries.assessment: The cross-product factor and sphere area are sound. Orthogonal spherical coordinates make the sine-of-angle factor too easy to overlook.
entries.change: Work a nonorthogonal parametrization, derive its Gram/cross-product area factor and address one-to-one coverage and patch addition explicitly. Label any convergence argument that remains a sketch.
entries.interaction: Link an actual parameter cell, tangent parallelogram and surface patch as cell size shrinks; display their area ratios.
entries.check: Derive dS for a new parametrization and explain why multiplying tangent lengths alone can fail.

entries.title: Integrate a density over a surface
entries.assessment: The sphere z² integral and graph formula are substantial content. The task asks for a separate paraboloid not represented by the sphere scene.
entries.change: Work the graph-surface derivation completely and add a nonconstant-density example with units. Explain reparametrization invariance and multiple coverage through concrete calculations.
entries.interaction: Provide the actual graph example as a selectable scene and distinguish density coloring from geometric height coloring.
entries.check: Compute a scalar surface integral and explain its independence from orientation but dependence on coverage multiplicity.

entries.title: Choose a continuous side
entries.assessment: Local versus global orientation and outward versus upward are well explained. A Möbius variant exists; it should be integrated with the textual argument rather than treated as decorative enrichment.
entries.change: Guide the transport of a normal around the Möbius seam and explain why the returned sign obstructs a global choice. Include cavity normals and connected versus disconnected surfaces.
entries.interaction: Use the existing sphere/Möbius variants for an explicit normal-transport task and an orientation reversal on orientable surfaces.
entries.check: Explain why two local normals at every point do not guarantee a continuous global normal field.
