entries.title: Flux measures normal flow
entries.assessment: The cancellation of normalization factors is correct, and the open-cap warning is important. A radial field on a sphere is too aligned to teach general flux.
entries.change: Add oblique and tangential fields, a graph patch and a cap-plus-disk calculation. Keep unit normal, scalar area factor and oriented area vector visibly distinct.
entries.interaction: Add normal reversal and cap-closure controls, with separate local dot product and accumulated signed flux.
entries.check: Set up flux with the requested orientation and account for every required surface component.

entries.title: Curl is oriented circulation density
entries.assessment: The curl/field-value distinction and factor-of-two angular-velocity caveat are excellent. A sampled arrow field does not by itself show the circulation-per-area limit.
entries.change: Derive a coordinate rectangle component in full, then explain other components and arbitrary oriented normals. Include shear as a contrast to rigid rotation.
entries.interaction: Shrink an oriented loop and display circulation, area and their ratio separately; retain exact derivative readouts.
entries.check: Interpret curl as a local oriented density rather than as arrow magnitude or the appearance of a global streamline.

entries.title: Divergence is local net outflow
entries.assessment: The dimensional generality and local-versus-finite-volume caveat are good. The radial/rotation slider does not expose the face-by-face cancellation in the definition.
entries.change: Work a small-box derivation and add a shear or balanced stretch/compression field. Explain divergence as the trace of the derivative matrix at an appropriate prerequisite level.
entries.interaction: Show opposing face fluxes and their total divided by volume while shrinking a box, with exact derivative comparison.
entries.check: Distinguish local divergence, finite-region flux and mere field magnitude.

entries.title: Successive derivatives cancel
entries.assessment: The identities are correct under the stated smoothness assumptions. Naming a cochain complex without developing spaces, linear maps, image/kernel and exactness risks turning enrichment into jargon.
entries.change: Expand one identity componentwise, then explain image⊆kernel and why equality is an additional claim. Put topology and cohomological interpretation in a clearly scaffolded optional track.
entries.interaction: Use linked operator diagrams and concrete fields rather than imply the generic arrow scene demonstrates an algebraic complex.
entries.check: Prove the cancellation identities and explain why zero consecutive composition does not by itself establish exactness.

entries.title: Stokes’ Theorem
entries.assessment: The compatible-orientation and entire-surface smoothness conditions are good. The simple paraboloid family is a useful invariance example but needs a genuine boundary-orientation exercise.
entries.change: Work a nonhorizontal boundary, a piecewise surface with an internal seam and two valid spanning surfaces. Separate the theorem statement from its pullback/Green proof sketch.
entries.interaction: Couple surface normal choices to induced boundary arrows and show patch-edge cancellation; track both sides of the equality during deformation.
entries.check: Choose an easier spanning surface only after checking smoothness and matching induced boundary orientation.

entries.title: Gauss–Ostrogradsky Divergence Theorem
entries.assessment: The singular radial-field caveat, cavity normals and cap-closure warning are all important and present. The symmetric sphere example is not enough method practice.
entries.change: Add a composite boundary with a closing disk, a cavity, and an off-center or nonsymmetric solid. Work each omitted-face correction explicitly.
entries.interaction: Show a closed/open indicator, every boundary component and its outward normals, with facewise flux and volume-integral totals.
entries.check: Apply the theorem only to a complete admissible boundary and subtract any artificially added surface correctly.

entries.title: Review: choose the correct integral theorem
entries.assessment: The four exact computations are useful, but some original problem data are only described as 'given' or 'supplied.' The canonical paraboloid does not represent all four geometries, and all answers are revealed together.
entries.change: Reproduce each problem's full original mathematical statement in original explanatory prose, then separate method choice, hypotheses, orientation, setup and solution. Include divergence/direct integration in a broader method chooser.
entries.interaction: Give each problem its own geometry or preloaded graph state; hide solutions until the learner commits to a method and sign.
entries.check: Solve each review problem from the site's statement alone, without needing an inaccessible source to discover the field or orientation.

entries.title: Review: straighten four curved boundaries
entries.assessment: The inverse map, negative determinant and area log(2)/2 check out. The generic linear scene does not visualize the exact curved boundary-straightening problem.
entries.change: Retain the computation but expand the choice of u=y/x³ and v=xy, inverse uniqueness and all boundary correspondences. Separate the signed determinant from the area factor.
entries.interaction: Render the exact first-quadrant region and parameter rectangle with paired cells and the varying factor 1/(4u).
entries.check: Derive the substitution from the boundaries and independently bound the area between 1/4 and 1/2.

entries.title: Review: the largest inscribed box
entries.assessment: The centering argument, logarithmic objective, boundary check and global conclusion are mathematically substantial and correct. The generic circle constraint scene cannot teach the ellipsoid/box geometry.
entries.change: Keep this as a model full application, expanding the half-length convention and comparison with normalized AM–GM. Explain the logarithm restriction before using it.
entries.interaction: Render the ellipsoid and its axis-aligned inscribed box, with full side lengths and volume changing together.
entries.check: Recover the global maximum 256/√3 while correctly distinguishing semiaxes, half-lengths and full side lengths.

entries.title: Review: classify all six stationary points
entries.assessment: The six points, values and Hessian signatures check out. Sending the learner to manually re-enter the expression in a separate graph studio breaks the review flow.
entries.change: Present a candidate table with gradient equations, Hessian signature, local type and global-status conclusion. Explain why the y³ term rules out absolute extrema on the whole plane.
entries.interaction: Provide a one-click preloaded exact surface and selectable critical points with local quadratic models and coordinate slices.
entries.check: Find and classify all six points, and explain why the local extrema are not global extrema.

entries.title: Review: the remainder decides differentiability
entries.assessment: Both exact review arguments are useful and correct: one uniform bound proves differentiability, while one diagonal defeats the other candidate. The generic scene is not the exact pair.
entries.change: Turn the two examples into a guided comparison: compute partials, identify the candidate, form the residual, then choose a uniform bound or obstruction. Keep the universal-quantifier distinction explicit.
entries.interaction: Plot the actual two functions with their own candidate planes and normalized remainders; use logarithmic radius steps to make scaling visible.
entries.check: Produce a complete differentiability proof for the first function and a valid counterexample path for the second.
